title: Transactions
lead: Transaction semantics, ACID, serial schedules, conflicts and serializability.
goals: ACID and the source interleaving example

sections.title: Transaction model and concurrent execution
sections.html:
Transactions as the unit of change

The earlier execution model assumed one user and no failures. Concurrent updates can race, and a power failure between debit and credit can lose money. Concurrency control and recovery address these problems around a transaction: an execution of operations representing one higher-level function.

BEGIN starts it; COMMIT accepts all its effects; ABORT/ROLLBACK removes its effects. The application can request abort, and the DBMS can force one. “All or nothing” describes the externally accepted result, not a claim that intermediate operations never run.

PDF pp. 1–5

Bank transfer and the database abstraction

The source transfers £100 between customer 1904’s Checking and Savings accounts. Between the two updates, the total is temporarily lower; transaction completion must restore the invariant. A funds check can be in application code or a stored procedure with variables, branches and loops, but it must participate in the concurrency-safe transaction rather than race with another debit.

BEGIN;
-- Check funds inside the protected transaction.
UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE customer_id = 1904 AND account_type = 'Checking';
UPDATE Accounts SET balance = balance + 100
WHERE customer_id = 1904 AND account_type = 'Savings';
COMMIT;

The DBMS abstracts a program into reads R(A) and writes W(A) on named objects, which can be attributes, records, pages or tables. Computation on retrieved values is not itself a database access. A database rollback does not automatically undo an email, cash dispensation or other outside-world action.

PDF pp. 6–9

Serial copying versus concurrent execution

A strawman runs one transaction at a time against a full database copy, replacing the original on success and discarding the copy on failure. Its simple reasoning comes at copying cost and low concurrency; a safe replacement still requires a crash-safe mechanism. The slide’s SQLite remark should not be read as a full description of its readers, writers and storage implementation.

Interleaving lets the CPU work while another transaction waits for I/O and can use multiple cores. It improves throughput and may reduce unrelated users’ latency, but scheduling must also preserve correctness and fairness.

PDF pp. 10–11

sections.title: ACID and the source interleaving example
sections.html:
ACID and its mechanisms

PropertyQuestion
AtomicityDid every action happen, or were all effects undone?
ConsistencyDoes the transaction preserve the intended integrity constraints?
IsolationIs the interleaving equivalent to the required isolated execution?
DurabilityWill acknowledged committed changes survive the specified failures?

Logging records enough information to undo aborted work and/or redo committed work; sequential log writes can be cheaper than forcing random data pages. Shadow paging changes copies and publishes a new page mapping at commit. Atomicity and durability require correct crash protocols, not merely a log file or copies.

Consistency includes schema constraints and application invariants. The application must make each standalone transaction preserve the intended invariant; the DBMS enforces declared constraints and the promised execution/recovery semantics. Isolation chooses admissible interleavings. Pessimistic control blocks conflicting work in advance; optimistic control validates and can roll back conflicting work later.

PDF pp. 12–17

Transfer plus interest: two serial results

Initially A=B=1000. T1 performs A−=100; B+=100. T2 applies 6% interest to both: A×=1.06; B×=1.06. T1 then T2 gives A=954,B=1166. T2 then T1 gives A=960,B=1160. Both totals are 2120; isolation does not require the same individual balances for these two serial orders.

The good interleaving debits A with T1, applies interest to A with T2, credits B with T1, then applies interest to B with T2. It yields 954,1166, matching T1→T2. Execution can overlap without changing the relevant effect of one serial order.

PDF pp. 18–21

The missing £6 and its read/write trace

The bad order debits A, applies interest to both accounts, then credits B. A=900×1.06=954, but B=1000×1.06+100=1160. Total 2114 misses the £6 interest on the transferred £100. It matches neither serial execution.

R1(A), W1(A), R2(A), W2(A), R2(B), W2(B), C2, R1(B), W1(B), C1

On A, T1 must precede T2; on B, T2 must precede T1. The database can detect this conflicting order without knowing the business meaning of interest.

PDF pp. 22–23

sections.title: Schedules and conflicting operations
sections.html:
Schedules, equivalence and serializability

A schedule interleaves all transactions’ operations while preserving each transaction’s internal order. A serial schedule completes one transaction before starting the next. Serializable means equivalent to some serial schedule, not necessarily transaction start order or commit order.

Equivalence must hold for the defined observations over all relevant initial states, rather than just accidentally producing the same number for one input. If every transaction preserves consistency when alone, serializable execution preserves it too. This gives a scheduler freedom to overlap work while retaining a useful correctness criterion.

PDF pp. 24–26

Three kinds of conflict

Operations conflict only if they belong to different transactions, touch the same object and at least one writes. Two reads commute for this test.

R–W: T1 reads A=10; T2 changes it to 19 and commits; T1 rereads 19—an unrepeatable read. W–R: T1 writes 12; T2 reads 12, derives 14 and commits; T1 aborts—T2 depended on an uncommitted value and cannot be justified by that aborted writer. W–W: transactions overwrite each other’s uncommitted A/B updates, potentially leaving a mixed final result. These are diagnostic patterns, not an instruction to forbid every conflict: serial executions also contain ordered conflicts.

PDF pp. 27–31

sections.title: Conflict serializability and precedence graphs
sections.html:
Conflict equivalence by adjacent swaps

Conflict-equivalent schedules contain the same operations and preserve the order of every conflicting pair. Adjacent non-conflicting operations from different transactions may be swapped. In the source animation, T1’s B operations move past T2’s A operations because A and B differ; repeated swaps collect all of T1 before T2. You must not swap operations within one transaction or reverse a same-object pair containing a write.

This provides a constructive witness of conflict serializability. The repeated animation pages are successive states of that argument, not six independent definitions.

PDF pp. 32–37

Precedence graphs and the cycle theorem

Create one vertex per transaction. For every earlier operation of Ti and later conflicting operation of Tj, add Ti→Tj; inspect all conflicting pairs, not only neighbouring operations. A schedule is conflict serializable iff this graph is acyclic.

A cycle requires each transaction to precede itself through a chain, impossible in a serial order. If acyclic, a topological ordering preserves every conflict edge and therefore supplies an equivalent serial order. Graph construction turns a cumbersome swap search into cycle detection.

PDF pp. 38–40

Two graph examples

Example one contains T1→T2 from one object and T2→T1 from the other: the two-cycle rejects conflict serializability. In the three-transaction example, the dependencies admit T2,T1,T3. T3 may start earlier than T2 but must occur later in the equivalent serial order. Start time alone supplies no serializability test.

PDF pp. 41–42

sections.title: View serializability and durability
sections.html:
View equivalence and blind writes

View equivalence preserves three observations for each object: which transaction reads its initial value; which writer supplies each read; and which transaction is the final writer. It can permit schedules rejected by conflict equivalence because a blind write need not preserve an overwritten value that nobody reads.

A concrete pattern is R1(A),W2(A),W1(A),W3(A): conflicts yield both T1→T2 and T2→T1, but view order T1,T2,T3 preserves T1’s initial read and T3’s final write. The other writes are blind or overwritten. Conflict-serializable schedules are a subset of view-serializable schedules; serial schedules are a subset of both. View serializability is harder to test/enforce, and these syntactic notions do not understand arbitrary application semantics. The source’s broad implementation claims are teaching context, not a survey proving every DBMS behaves alike.

PDF pp. 43–46

Durability and the division of responsibility

Once commit is acknowledged, accepted changes must survive the failures covered by the storage protocol. Torn updates and surviving aborted changes must be addressed by recovery. Logging and shadow paging support this guarantee. Concurrency control selects admissible interleavings; recovery restores the accepted transaction outcome after aborts and failures. ACID is a collection of distinct obligations, not four names for locking.

PDF pp. 47–48

quiz.question: Is R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B) conflict-serializable?
options: Yes, in the order T1 then T2
Yes, in the order T2 then T1
No, because the graph has a cycle
There is insufficient information because two objects are involved
quiz.explanation: Both R1(A) before W2(A) and W1(B) before R2(B) create T1 → T2. There is no edge in the reverse direction.

source.summary: Lecture 19 introduces transactions, ACID, execution schedules, conflicts, and two serializability criteria. A dependency graph checks conflict serializability, while logging or shadow paging supports atomicity and durability.
